tier_reason: The independent qpbenchmark dense report (public code, i7-6500U, PyPI solver versions, no compiler flags) lists Clarabel and ECOS, but its 6x runtime gap is a success-rate artifact: every failure is charged the 1000 s limit, no Clarabel or ECOS run in results/qpbenchmark_results.csv takes more than 0.07 s, ECOS's failures come from qpsolvers' QP-to-SOCP conversion (open fairness issue #60 listed under the report's Known limitations), and on the 9 dense problems both solve ECOS is faster (derived from page data). With the independent data not supporting a speed win, the remaining speed claim is first-party (README without numbers, paper seen only as a search snippet), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Dense-subset (62 problems) runtime scores are shifted geometric means normalised to the best solver (PIQP = 1.0), not seconds: default Clarabel 20793.9 vs ECOS 126497.0 (6.1x lower, derived from page data); high accuracy 20.1 vs 112.3 (5.6x); mid accuracy 116.6 vs 652.7 (5.6x); low accuracy 26095.2 vs 171259.8 (6.6x). Success rate at default 51.6% vs 12.9% (high accuracy 43.5% vs 0.0%). These gaps measure failures charged at the 1000 s limit, not solve speed: in results/qpbenchmark_results.csv every ECOS dense run ends within 0.03 s and every Clarabel dense run within 0.07 s, and on the 9 dense problems both solvers solve at default settings ECOS is faster on geometric mean (ECOS/Clarabel time 0.84, about 1.19x in ECOS's favour; derived from page data). Clarabel wins DUAL1-DUAL4, DUALC1 and DUALC5 by 1.05-1.55x and loses HS118, HS21 and HS53 by 1.6-4.8x; the same commonly-solved comparison gives ECOS/Clarabel ratios of 0.84 (high), 0.88 (mid) and 0.94 (low accuracy). On the full 138-problem set at default Clarabel (163.8) trails PIQP (1.0), QPALM (3.6), OSQP (12.7), SCS (15.1), HiGHS (30.7), ProxQP (53.3) and CVXOPT (94.1); ECOS is not run there.
corrections.caveats: Not faster than ECOS on solve time in this suite: the 6x shifted-geometric-mean gap is produced by failures charged at the 1000 s limit, and ECOS fails 53 of 62 dense problems within milliseconds because qpsolvers converts each QP to an SOCP through a NumPy Cholesky factorisation that needs a positive definite P (qpbenchmark issue #60, open, labelled fairness: 'failing to solve the problem is no fault of the solver itself'). On the problems both solve, ECOS is faster on geometric mean (derived from results/qpbenchmark_results.csv). Clarabel's own failures also end in milliseconds (no timeouts), so its 51.6% success rate is low for an interior-point solver; the cause was not investigated. The report also lists CPU thermal throttling (#88) as a known limitation. Python wrapper and qpsolvers conversion overhead are included for every solver. Clarabel trails OSQP (C), SCS (C), HiGHS (C++), PIQP (C++) and others on the full and sparse sets. The broader 'faster than commercial and open-source solvers on QPs' claim is from the Goulart and Chen paper (arXiv 2405.12762, Mathematical Programming Computation per a search snippet; neither arxiv.org nor the Oxford repository copy could be opened), so its numbers are unverified. ClarabelBenchmarks (oxfordcontrol) holds the authors' benchmark code but commits no result tables.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated by the benchmark. Solvers are PyPI builds (clarabel 0.9.0, ecos 2.0.14) called from Python 3.12.4 through qpsolvers 4.3.3; ecos-python's setup.py passes no extra_compile_args (setuptools defaults of the Python build), and Clarabel.rs's Cargo.toml does not override the release profile.
corrections.hardware: Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-6500U CPU @ 2.50GHz (4 logical CPUs), benchmark version 2.3.0 run 2024-09-07 by the qpbenchmark author (@stephane-caron); thermal throttling listed as known limitation #88
corrections.why_faster: README: unlike standard HSDE interior-point solvers, Clarabel handles quadratic objectives without an epigraphical reformulation. In this suite that difference shows up as robustness, not speed: ECOS only sees the QP after qpsolvers' SOCP conversion, which fails for positive semidefinite P, while on the problems ECOS does receive and solve it is faster than Clarabel on geometric mean. The comparison is algorithm against algorithm, not a Rust-versus-C language effect.

notes: Keep with shortcoming 'not faster than ECOS on commonly solved problems; 6x figure is a failure-penalty artifact of qpsolvers' QP-to-SOCP conversion (qpbenchmark #60)'. The record had the high- and low-accuracy figures swapped (20.1 vs 112.3 is high accuracy, 26095.2 vs 171259.8 is low accuracy); fixed in claimed_speedup. Per-problem ratios were derived from results/qpbenchmark_results.csv in the same repo. Metadata checked: 617 stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-04-13, not a fork.

tier_reason: The only numbers are one first-party @btime pair in the README (698.611 ns vs 5.433 us for N=64 SVector), with no CPU, Julia version or FFTW build stated; the repo's benchmark/ suite has no committed results (its report lives in 30-day CI artifacts and the github.io docs, not reachable here), so C.

corrections.caveats: Single cherry-picked README snippet (the author says so), no CPU, Julia version, FFTW_jll build or flags. Both calls go through AbstractFFTs' one-shot path, fft(x, region) = (y = to1(x); plan_fft(y, region) * y), so a plan is built on every call; for FFTW that means the FFTW planner runs per call on a copy of the SVector (complexfloat copies it into a ComplexF64 Array), so the 7.8x mostly measures planning and conversion overhead, not transform speed. FFTW with a reused plan is not compared, and the README itself sends users wanting performance to FFTW.jl. The repo's benchmark/ suite (separate Julia environments, fft($x) with a fresh plan per call, sizes up to 32768 and primes to 20000) commits no results; reports are CI artifacts kept 30 days and a docs page on github.io. Not a general speedup claim and not a Julia-versus-C codegen result.
corrections.why_faster: Per-call overhead, not the transform kernel: the one-shot fft builds a plan on every call, and FFTW's planner plus the SVector-to-Array conversion cost more at N=64 than FFTA's generic Julia plan, which specialises on the StaticArrays input. The README gives only type specialisation as the reason; FFTW's codelets are a different algorithm from FFTA's generic mixed-radix code.

notes: Keep at C with shortcoming 'single cherry-picked one-shot timing at N=64 where FFTW's per-call planning dominates; no reused-plan comparison, no methodology'. Numbers match the README exactly; metadata checked (76 stars, MIT, last commit 2026-09-01, JuliaMath org, not a fork). Close to the crippled-baseline line (FFTW used without plan reuse), but both sides use the same one-shot API, so C rather than D.

tier_reason: First-party ITensor benchmark repo with public code for both sides (src/bench_*/runbenchmark.jl and runbenchmark.h, src/runbenchmarks.jl) and raw timings under data/, but no CPU model, no Julia version and only a sample options.mk for the C++ build; the SciPost Codebases paper (Section 12.1 compares the Julia and C++ versions) was seen only as a search snippet, so C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: C++ side per deps/options.mk.sample: g++ -m64 -std=c++17 -fconcepts -fPIC with OPTIMIZATIONS=-O2 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wno-unknown-pragmas, ITENSOR_USE_OMP=1 (-fopenmp), MKL (-lmkl_intel_lp64 -lmkl_intel_thread -lmkl_rt -lmkl_core -liomp5 -lpthread); the options.mk actually used is not committed. Julia side: version and flags not stated (data directory named v0.1.37, the ITensors.jl release); the runner checks that Julia's BLAS vendor matches and disables Strided.jl threads. C++ runs with MKL_NUM_THREADS and OMP_NUM_THREADS set to the thread counts in the data path.
corrections.caveats: Numbers read from the raw .txt files under data/ (for example data/c++/v3.1.6/bench_dmrg_2d_conserve_ky/blas_num_threads_1/blocksparse_num_threads_1/maxdim_10000.txt and the same path under data/julia/v0.1.37); every cited figure matches. Same model, sweeps, maxdim schedule, noise, zero cutoff and initial state on both sides, and ITensors.jl v0.1.37's eigsolve_krylovdim 3 / maxiter 1 is documented in its dmrg.jl as equivalent to C++ Niter 2, so the work is matched. Timing asymmetry: Julia is warmed up first (maxdim 10, 2 sweeps) and timed with @elapsed in-process, while C++ is timed with @elapsed around a bash script that launches the binary, so C++ rows include process start and library loading (matters only for the sub-second TRG/CTMRG rows). C++ built at -O2 (sample options), not -O3, though large-bond-dimension time is dominated by MKL on both sides. No CPU model for this data (the TeNPy comparison page in the same repo names 4 x Xeon Gold 6128 for its own runs only). Data from February 2021 (benchmark repo last commit 2021-12-06, stale); ITensors.jl has since been rewritten around NDTensors and C++ ITensor has moved on. Single runs, no variance. Julia is not uniformly faster: it loses at small bond dimension (TRG maxdim 10 1.11 s vs 0.16 s, CTMRG maxdim 50 2.33 s vs 0.92 s, DMRG 2D QN maxdim 1000 405.8 s vs 334.8 s). The SciPost Phys. Codebases 4 (2022) paper (arXiv 2007.14822) has a Julia-versus-C++ benchmark section per a search snippet; scipost.org and arxiv.org were not reachable, so its figures were not checked against these data.
corrections.why_faster: Not stated by the sources. Both sides call MKL with one thread, and at large bond dimension the run time is dominated by MKL GEMM, SVD and eigensolver calls, so the Julia lead there comes from library-level differences in block-sparse contraction and tensor handling between ITensors.jl v0.1.37 and C++ ITensor v3.1.6, not from compiler codegen; the benchmark does not isolate the cause.

notes: Keep at C with shortcomings 'first-party, no CPU model, C++ at -O2 from a sample options file, C++ timing includes process launch, stale 2021 data, Julia slower at small bond dimension'. All cited numbers verified against the raw data files; same_algorithm confirmed from the paired benchmark sources. Metadata checked: 686 stars, Apache-2.0, last commit 2026-09-27, not a fork.
